15  Forecast evaluation

  • Show All Code

Every forecaster from rolling origins 1900–2015, horizons 1–50, each fitted to the data up to its origin

NotePaper correspondence

Paper §10 (“Forecast Evaluation”), and the forecasting results quoted in the abstract, §1 and §11.3. The design was written down and frozen, before any of this chapter’s numbers existed, and revised in its overall comparison (Deviation 2) and corrected (Deviation 3) after independent reviews (this chapter’s record; the article gives the final form only). Produces the table tbl-ev-overall (§10.6). The rest is in the companion only: the table tbl-ev-design and the figures fig-ev-curves, fig-ev-overall and fig-ev-arriaga; the runs and the pooling, tbl-ev-runtime and tbl-ev-pooling; accuracy and bias by horizon band, tbl-ev-bands, tbl-ev-bias-bands, tbl-ev-cellbias and tbl-ev-bias; the intervals, the figure fig-ev-coverage and the tables tbl-ev-coverage-rule, tbl-ev-past-intervals and tbl-ev-coverage; the overall comparison in detail, tbl-ev-smaa, tbl-ev-smaa-weights, tbl-ev-pairwise, tbl-ev-perpop, tbl-ev-family-corr, tbl-ev-measures-window, tbl-ev-measures and tbl-ev-robust; the sensitivity analyses, tbl-ev-sensitivity, tbl-ev-jumpoff, tbl-ev-ensemble-naive and tbl-ev-paired; tbl-ev-overall-frozen; the variants, tbl-ev-variants-forms, tbl-ev-held-forms, tbl-ev-ablation, tbl-ev-mdmx-sens, tbl-ev-variants-measures and tbl-ev-lilee; and generality and diagnostics, tbl-ev-generality, tbl-ev-rho, tbl-ev-positions and the figures fig-ev-frontier, fig-ev-window and fig-ev-pace. Also produces every \ev… macro.

This chapter compares the two forecasters of chapter 11, MDMx with its jump-off anchor and the flow field, with the established methods: Lee–Carter, Hyndman–Ullah’s functional model, the coherent functional model, and the UN’s bayesLife, each fitted either to every year of a population’s history or to its last 50 years. An equally weighted ensemble of anchored MDMx, the flow field and Lee–Carter on the last 50 years is the twelfth entry. A random walk with drift is the yardstick that scales every measure.

The design was frozen before any of its numbers existed: the origins, the entries, the views, the measures and the rule that names the headline (paper §10.5). Not everything stayed as frozen. After the comparison and the held-out block had first been scored, independent reviews found that the frozen overall comparison counted the level of e₀ in overlapping families, rewarded errors that offset, and scored intervals calibrated in different ways. The overall comparison was revised (Deviation 2), and the corrections of four further reviews followed (Deviation 3: life expectancy from death rates with a₀ = 0.3 at age 0, the book’s life-table convention). Deviation 3 changed the entries that convert death rates: Lee–Carter, Hyndman–Ullah and the coherent model, bayesLife (whose input series changed, so its runs were all made again) and, through Lee–Carter, the ensemble. Anchored MDMx, the flow field and the naive convert no rates and did not change. This chapter reports the revised and corrected comparison; the frozen one is kept beside it as the record of that path. Because the revision came after the held-out block had been scored, the block is not a blind test of the revised comparison.

def _word(n):
    """An integer 1–99 as a macro-name word: 5 → Five, 25 → Twentyfive."""

class _BandTag(dict):
    """Band label → macro-name tag, "16–25" → "SixteenTwentyfive"; a band cut at the data's last year
    ("16–20" when the held-out block reaches 20 years) gets its own tag the same way."""

    def __missing__(self, label):
        lo, hi = (int(x) for x in label.split("–"))
        return _word(lo) + _word(hi)

def formats(df, digits, ints=()):
    """Number formats for a paper table: ``digits`` decimals with a true minus sign (``latex.fmt_num``, as
    every other table), whole numbers with thousands separators for the ``ints`` columns."""
    return {c: (latex.fmt_int if c in ints else (lambda v, d=digits: latex.fmt_num(v, d))) for c in df.columns
            if pd.api.types.is_numeric_dtype(df[c])}


def shown_name(label):
    """An entry's label as the article writes it ("MDMx + anchor, all years" → "Anchored MDMx, all years").
    The analysis keeps its own labels: they name the runs, the ensemble's members and the macros."""
    return label.replace("MDMx + anchor", "Anchored MDMx")


def save_table(df, label, caption, **kwargs):
    """``latex.save_table`` with every text cell's entry names as the article writes them (:func:`shown_name`)."""
    out = df.copy()
    for c in [c for c in out.columns if not pd.api.types.is_numeric_dtype(out[c])]:
        out[c] = out[c].map(lambda v: shown_name(v) if isinstance(v, str) else v)
    return latex.save_table(out, label, caption, **kwargs)


def ranked(df, best="min", columns=None, stub="Entry", exclude=(ev.NAIVE,), **kwargs):
    """The comparison of a paper table (``latex.Rank``): every numeric column, or ``columns``, among the rows
    whose ``stub`` is not in ``exclude`` (the naive is the yardstick, not an entry).  A dict ``best`` (column →
    what is better) names the columns itself."""
    columns = columns or (list(best) if isinstance(best, dict) else
                          [c for c in df.columns if pd.api.types.is_numeric_dtype(df[c])])
    return latex.Rank(columns, best, rows=list(~df[stub].isin(exclude)), **kwargs)


def band_columns(df):
    """The horizon-band columns of a table (under the spanner "Years ahead")."""
    return [c for c in df.columns if isinstance(c, str) and c.startswith("Years ahead: ")]


# What one comparison is, after the caption's key to the marks (latex.Rank).
RANK_ERA = "among the twelve entries, in each column of each era (the naive is not ranked)"
RANK_BANDS = "in each column of each group, the best being the smallest MAE and the mean error closest to zero"


def ranked_bands(df, group="Group", stub="Entry", exclude=(ev.NAIVE,)):
    """The comparisons of a band table whose row groups hold MAEs or mean errors: the smallest MAE, the mean
    error closest to zero, among the rows whose ``stub`` is not in ``exclude``."""
    bias = df[group].str.startswith("Mean error")
    keep = ~df[stub].isin(exclude)
    return [latex.Rank(band_columns(df), "min", rows=list(keep & ~bias)),
            latex.Rank(band_columns(df), "zero", rows=list(keep & bias))]


def years_ahead(df):
    """Horizon-band columns ("1–5", "16–25") under one spanner, "Years ahead"."""
    return df.rename(columns={c: f"Years ahead: {c}" for c in df.columns
                              if isinstance(c, str) and re.fullmatch(r"\d+–\d+", c)})


def grouped_bands(df, stub):
    """A long band table (Measure, Era, ``stub``, bands) as the table standard sets it: one row group per
    measure and era, the bands under one spanner."""
    out = df.copy()
    out.insert(0, "Group", [f"{MEASURE_NAME.get(m, m)}, {ERA_SHORT[e]}"
                            for m, e in zip(out["Measure"], out["Era"], strict=True)])
    return years_ahead(out.drop(columns=["Measure", "Era"]))


def report_band(lo, hi, what):
    """A horizon band as a text macro for the paper: ``evBandOneFive`` → 1--5."""
    label = f"{lo}–{hi}"
    latex.report(f"evBand{BAND_TAG[label]}", label, text=f"{lo}--{hi}", desc=f"Horizons {label} (years): {what}")


def num(key):
    """A registered number as plain text for the prose of this book."""
    return latex.reported()[key]["text"].replace("{,}", ",").replace("$-$", "−")


def val(key):
    """A registered number's value, for a comparison in the prose."""
    return float(latex.reported()[key]["value"])

15.1 The design

Forecasts are made from an origin every five years from 1900 to 2015 (paper §10.1). A population is forecast from an origin if it has at least 30 observed years up to the origin and 3 after it, and each forecast runs 50 years. The origins form three groups:

  • the early era, 1900–1950, outside the regime of modern mortality decline: the out-of-regime check;
  • the late era, 1955–2000: the primary view. With the early era it forms the development origins, on which the flow field’s pace beyond the frontier point was chosen;
  • the held-out block, 2005–2015, held out from every formal choice of form and design. It had not gone unseen: the first development study, which chose the flow field’s relaxation form and the persistent anchor, used origins up to 2010; a later study reported errors at 2005–2015 for the methods of the time; and bayesLife had been run from 2010. The block was scored once, by a run that changed nothing else, before the overall comparison was revised. It reaches at most 20 years ahead (the origin 2015 at most 10).

Truth is the HMD’s observed e₀ in normal years: the years of the event dictionary (chapter d3) are left out of the scoring, among them wars, 1918, and three pandemics masked in every population whether or not its mortality rose there: the influenza pandemics of 1957–58 and 1968–69, and COVID-19 (counts below). Every comparison is made on the same points: the population-years at which every entry forecasts both sexes and their average, and all three are observed.

15.2 The runs

Every entry is run at every origin under each of its fitting periods, and each model is fitted only to data for years up to its origin, taken from the HMD release this book uses (29 October 2026, chapter d1), not the data available at the time. The forecasts are therefore out of sample from rolling origins; they are not the forecasts that could have been made at the time, which would have used the data then available. A few inputs draw on data for years after the origin, and they are listed here in one place (paper §10.9):

  • pooling: at the ages where small populations record zero deaths, the data pipeline pools deaths and exposures over blocks of adjacent years formed on the whole series, so a block can span an origin (counts below);
  • intervals: the comparison’s intervals are calibrated on the errors at the other origins of the era, later ones included (intervals from past errors only are reported beside them);
  • bayesLife: its default priors come from WPP data that extend beyond most origins, and the σ of its gap model’s second equation is bayesLife’s own WPP-derived value at the origins up to 1990;
  • MortCast: the rotation of bayesLife’s schedules uses MortCast’s default rotation settings, estimated on recent data;
  • the age rank of the decomposition (chapter 04) was chosen on all the data;
  • MDMx’s settings (the drift weights and the number of components) were set before this evaluation, on data that include years after most origins (alternatives are reported below);
  • the event dictionary marks the crisis years with hindsight, and the truth leaves them out;
  • which populations are scored: a population enters an origin’s jobs only if it is observed for at least 3 years after the origin, and the jobs also decide which populations form bayesLife’s world level (and Li–Lee’s group, below).

The exceptions touch different entries: bayesLife’s priors and MortCast’s rotation the comparators, the age rank the two new forecasters, MDMx’s settings MDMx, the pooling the entries trained on pooled data, and the intervals every entry (their bias adjustment helps most the entries with a persistent bias). Their effects are not measured, except for MDMx’s settings and the intervals, whose alternatives are reported below. Chapter 11 describes the two forecasters. The comparators run in R, through the package demography (R/demography_forecasts.R, settings in config/params.d/forecast.toml): Lee–Carter on each sex’s rates, with k_t refitted to the observed total deaths (adjust = "dt", as Lee and Carter 1992); Hyndman–Ullah’s functional model on the rates smoothed year by year; and the coherent functional model, which forecasts the product and the ratio of the sexes’ smoothed rates. The runs are cached per origin; tools/warm_evaluation.py computes the same runs ahead of a render. bayesLife’s 48 runs (24 origins, two fitting periods) are made off-site, in a project that tools/bayeslife_bundle.py writes from the book’s own inputs and R scripts (R/bayeslife_forecast.R and its patches); they are imported below after checks that they are the book’s own runs.

Every run but bayesLife’s (cached per origin; computed ahead by tools/warm_evaluation.py)

The R warnings all come from Lee–Carter’s lca. Where a small population has no deaths at some age in some year, the log rate is infinite: lca replaces it (“Inf replaced by maximum positive value”) or estimates the zero rate (“Replacing zero values with estimates”). “No root exists. Returning closest” means that in some year no k_t reproduces the observed deaths exactly, and lca keeps the closest value. These are the package’s documented behaviour; no forecast is missing because of them.

15.2.1 bayesLife: the off-site runs

The off-site project’s runs, gathered from the machines that made them, are copied into work/bayeslife/chapter-12-input/ by tools/fetch_bayeslife_offsite.py. Each run is accepted only if the project’s files match its manifest, the run finished, and its input e₀ and settings are byte-for-byte those the book itself would have sent (bayeslife.offsite_runs). bayesLife forecasts e₀ only; its schedules come from its median e₀ path by MortCast’s coherent rotated Lee–Carter, fitted to each population’s smoothed rates over the job’s fitting window. MortCast matches e₀ in its own life table (a₀ by Andreev and Kingkade, ages to 130), whose e₀ differs from the book’s (a₀ = 0.3) where infant mortality is high. The schedules are scored in the book’s life table, so MortCast’s target is moved by the remaining difference until the schedules’ e₀ there is bayesLife’s median, to 0.025 years (MortCast itself meets its target to 0.01 years).

bayesLife: import the off-site runs, check them, MortCast schedules 
# bayesLife's inputs first: tools/bayeslife_bundle.py writes the runs from this artefact.
e0_bl = artifacts.stage("forecast_bl_e0", lambda: bl.e0_series(ctx["rates"], A, ctx["cmp"]["mx_to_qx_ax"]),
                        inputs=["forecast_cmp_rates"], params={"n_ages": A, "ax": ctx["cmp"]["mx_to_qx_ax"]},
                        code=[bl.e0_series, fc.comparator_schedules, fc.e0_and_gradient],
                        desc="Female and male e0 of every population-year of the comparators' rates")
BL_FOLDER = paths.bayeslife() / "chapter-12-input"
if not (BL_FOLDER / "MANIFEST.json").is_file():
    raise FileNotFoundError(f"{paths.relative(BL_FOLDER)} is missing: write and run a bayesLife batch "
                            "(tools/bayeslife_bundle.py), then copy it there (tools/fetch_bayeslife_offsite.py); "
                            "the README says how ('Run bayesLife for chapter 12')")
BL_RUNS = bl.offsite_runs(BL_FOLDER, e0_bl, ctx["jobs"], FAMILY, ctx["names"], horizon=D.horizon,
                          settings=F["bayeslife"], e0_artefact="forecast_bl_e0")
BL_SCHED = ev.run_bl_schedules(BL_RUNS, ctx["smoothed"], ctx["jobs"], n_ages=A, ax=ctx["cmp"]["mx_to_qx_ax"],
                               e0_tol=float(E["bl_schedule_e0_tol"]), max_rounds=int(E["bl_schedule_max_rounds"]),
                               name="evaluation_blsched", concurrent=CONCURRENT)
bl_summary = pd.DataFrame([
    {"policy": p, "origin": o, **{k: v for k, v in bl.run_summary(r, ctx["jobs"][p][ctx["jobs"][p]["origin"] == o],
                                                                FAMILY).items() if np.isscalar(v)},
     "hours": r["provenance"]["hours"]}
    for (p, o), r in sorted(BL_RUNS.items())])
bl_e0_gap = pd.concat([s["e0_check"].assign(policy=p, origin=o) for (p, o), s in BL_SCHED.items()],
                      ignore_index=True)
bl_e0_gap = np.maximum((bl_e0_gap["female"] - bl_e0_gap["female_bl"]).abs(), (bl_e0_gap["male"] - bl_e0_gap["male_bl"]).abs())
latex.report("evBlRuns", len(BL_RUNS), desc="bayesLife runs imported (origins × fitting periods)")
latex.report("evBlHours", bl_summary["hours"].sum(), digits=1, desc="bayesLife run-hours, all runs")
latex.report("evBlMortcastGapMax", float(bl_e0_gap.max()), digits=3,
             desc="Largest |e0 of the MortCast schedule − bayesLife median| (book life table, years)")
bl_rounds = pd.Series({k: s["rounds"] for k, s in BL_SCHED.items()})
print(f"{len(BL_RUNS)} runs, {bl_summary['hours'].sum():.1f} run-hours; MortCast schedules' e₀ (book life table) "
      f"within {bl_e0_gap.max():.4f} y of the median after at most {bl_rounds.max()} further MortCast calls")
# A run is extended until it meets the convergence rule, up to a fixed number of extensions; the runs that
# reached that number without meeting it are scored as they ended.
BL_NOT_CONVERGED = bl_summary[~bl_summary["converged"].astype(bool)]
latex.report("evBlNotConverged", len(BL_NOT_CONVERGED),
             desc="bayesLife runs that ended without meeting the convergence rule (scored as they ended)")
latex.report("evBlNotConvergedEarly", int(BL_NOT_CONVERGED["origin"].isin(D.eras["early"]).sum()),
             desc="Of those, the runs at early-era origins")
# Equation 2 of the gap model takes bayesLife's WPP-derived sigma where the data up to the origin have no
# female e0 above its threshold: at every origin up to a last one, for both fitting periods.
BL_WPP_LAST = int(bl_summary.loc[bl_summary["eq2_wpp"].astype(bool), "origin"].max())
if not (bl_summary["eq2_wpp"].astype(bool) == (bl_summary["origin"] <= BL_WPP_LAST)).all():
    raise ValueError("equation 2's WPP sigma is not used at exactly the origins up to the last one that uses it")
latex.report("evBlWppSigmaLastOrigin", BL_WPP_LAST, text=latex.fmt_year(BL_WPP_LAST),
             desc="The last origin at which bayesLife's gap model takes equation 2's sigma from the WPP (issue BL-3)")
print("Runs that did not meet the convergence rule (policy-origin: extensions):",
      ", ".join(f"{r.policy}-{r.origin}: {r.steps}" for r in BL_NOT_CONVERGED.itertuples()) or "none")

The correction of Deviation 3 is at age 0. Before it, the comparators turned their death rates into probabilities of dying with a₀ = 0.5, the a_x they use above age 0, while the book’s life table uses a₀ = 0.3; bayesLife was fitted to e₀ series converted in the same way. The difference matters where infant mortality is high. Its size, on the comparators’ own input rates of the years before 1950:

The size of the age-0 correction, on the comparators’ input rates 
# Each population-year's rates as the comparators receive them, ages 0 to their open age: an age with no
# exposure keeps the rate of the age below (as bl.e0_series), and the open group's rate holds at every
# older age (as fc.comparator_schedules).
_r = ctx["rates"][ctx["rates"]["year"] < int(E["a0_offset_before"])]
_m = (_r.assign(mx=_r["deaths"] / _r["exposure"].where(_r["exposure"] > 0))
      .pivot(index=["pop", "year", "sex"], columns="age", values="mx").ffill(axis=1))
_mx = _m.to_numpy()
if not np.isfinite(_mx).all():
    raise ValueError("a population-year of the comparators' rates has no rate at some age")
_mx = np.concatenate([_mx[:, :-1], np.repeat(_mx[:, -1:], A - _mx.shape[1] + 1, axis=1)], axis=1)  # (N, A)
CMP_AX, BOOK_A0 = float(ctx["cmp"]["mx_to_qx_ax"]), float(P.section("data")["a0"])


def e0_converted(a0):
    """e₀ in the book's life table of the rates ``_mx`` converted to q_x with ``a0`` at age 0."""
    return lifetable.e0_from_qx(lifetable.qx_from_mx(_mx, lifetable.conversion_ax(A, CMP_AX, a0=a0)), a0=BOOK_A0)


# The change of e₀, the average of the sexes, in the population-years with both sexes.
A0_SHIFT = (pd.Series(e0_converted(BOOK_A0) - e0_converted(CMP_AX), index=_m.index)
            .unstack("sex").dropna().mean(axis=1))
latex.report("evAzeroOffsetEarly", float(A0_SHIFT.median()), digits=2,
             desc=f"Median rise of e0 (average of the sexes) from a0 = {CMP_AX:g} to the book's a0 at age 0, the "
                  f"comparators' input rates before {int(E['a0_offset_before'])}")
print(f"{len(A0_SHIFT):,} population-years before {E['a0_offset_before']}: e₀ rises by a median "
      f"{A0_SHIFT.median():.3f} y (5th–95th percentile {A0_SHIFT.quantile(0.05):.3f}–{A0_SHIFT.quantile(0.95):.3f})")
1,542 population-years before 1950: e₀ rises by a median 0.155 y (5th–95th percentile 0.019–0.446)

With a₀ = 0.5 the comparators’ e₀ (the average of the sexes) was a median of 0.15 years lower in these years than in the book’s life table.

15.2.2 The entries on common points

The ensemble is the equally weighted mean of its members’ e₀ forecasts and of their logit(q_x) schedules, where all three members forecast. Every comparison below is made on the points at which all twelve entries forecast both sexes and their average, and all three are observed.

Every entry’s points and schedules; the naive; the common points; errors 
results = ev.entry_results(ctx, runs, BL_RUNS, BL_SCHED)
points = ev.long_points(results)
naive_q = cp.naive_e0(truth, ctx["jobs"]["full"], LEVELS)
points = pd.concat([points, naive_q.assign(entry=ev.NAIVE, h=naive_q["year"] - naive_q["origin"])
                    [["entry", "pop", "sex", "origin", "year", "h", "e0_fc"]]], ignore_index=True)
points["era"] = points["origin"].map(ERA_OF)
keys_all = ev.paired_keys(points, truth, ENTRIES + [ev.NAIVE])
keys_all["era"] = keys_all["origin"].map(ERA_OF)
# The held-out block is scored only when the design switches it on (score_held_out).
keys = keys_all if HELD else keys_all[keys_all["era"] != "held"].reset_index(drop=True)
errs = ev.errors(points, truth, keys)
errs["era"] = errs["origin"].map(ERA_OF)
n_expected = points[(points["entry"] == ev.NAIVE) & (points["sex"] == "both")].merge(
    truth[truth["sex"] == "both"], on=["pop", "year"])
n_expected = n_expected[n_expected["origin"].map(D.era) != "held"] if not HELD else n_expected
latex.report("evNPoints", len(keys), desc="Common points (population-years) scored")
for era in ERAS_ALL if HELD else D.eras:
    latex.report(f"evNPoints{era.capitalize()}", int((keys["era"] == era).sum()), desc=f"Common points, {era} era")
print(f"Common points: {len(keys):,} of {len(n_expected):,} observed naive points "
      f"({100 * len(keys) / len(n_expected):.1f} %); by era: {keys['era'].value_counts().to_dict()}")

# The truth leaves out every year of the event dictionary (chapter d3).  Three pandemics are masked in every
# population with data, whether or not its mortality rose: 1957–58 and 1968–69 are disclosed as such, COVID-19
# beside them.
HAS_DATA = np.isfinite(M).all(axis=(0, 1))                       # (C, T): the masked years keep their data
masked_jobs = ctx["jobs"]["full"][ctx["jobs"]["full"]["origin"].map(ERA_OF).isin(ERAS)]
MASKED = va.masked_event_counts(dt.load_events().query("populations == 'ALL'"), HAS_DATA, observed, years, pops,
                                masked_jobs, D.horizon)
for r_ in MASKED.itertuples():
    tag = "".join(w.capitalize() for w in "".join(ch for ch in r_.event if ch.isalpha() or ch == " ").split())
    latex.report(f"evMasked{tag}PopYears", int(r_.popyears),
                 desc=f"Population-years masked from the truth in every population: {r_.event} {r_.start}-{r_.end}")
    latex.report(f"evMasked{tag}Points", int(r_.forecast),
                 desc=f"Forecast years (job × year, scored eras) in those population-years, not scored: {r_.event}")
MASKED_TAB = MASKED.assign(years=MASKED["start"].astype(str) + "–" + MASKED["end"].astype(str))[
    ["event", "years", "popyears", "forecast"]].rename(columns={"popyears": "population-years masked",
                                                                 "forecast": "forecast years not scored"})
print("Events masked in every population with data:\n" + MASKED_TAB.to_string(index=False))
Common points: 15,261 of 15,261 observed naive points (100.0 %); by era: {'late': 8763, 'early': 5347, 'held': 1151}
Events masked in every population with data:
              event     years  population-years masked  forecast years not scored
    Asian influenza 1957–1958                       63                        250
Hong Kong influenza 1968–1969                       78                        270
           COVID-19 2020–2022                      108                        776

The influenza pandemics of 1957–58 and 1968–69 are masked in every population with data: 63 and 78 population-years, in which 250 and 270 forecast years of the scored eras go unscored. The models are fitted without them too. Chapter 08 estimates no excess (a negative intensity) for many respiratory event-years, so masking these two pandemics in every population is a choice, not a finding; a sensitivity analysis that keeps them has not yet been made.

15.3 Accuracy by era and horizon

The mean absolute error of e₀ (the average of the sexes) in each horizon band (paper §10.3), on the common points. The late era is the primary view; the early era, outside the regime the forms were chosen in, is reported with the same prominence. Few origins reach the longest horizons (in the late era only those up to 1985 reach 36–50 years), so the right-hand columns rest on few forecasts; every claim beyond 20 years is descriptive (the held-out block reaches no further).

Code 
both_err = errs[errs["measure"] == "e0_both"]
bands = ev.band_table(both_err, D, ["entry", "era"])
band_tab = (bands.pivot_table(index="entry", columns=["era", "band"], values="mae", observed=True)
            .reindex(index=ENTRIES + [ev.NAIVE]))
band_tab = band_tab.reindex(columns=pd.MultiIndex.from_product([ERAS, BANDS]))
# A band as scored: the held-out block reaches only H_MAX["held"] years ahead, so its last band is labelled by
# the horizons it holds (16–20 on the data to 2025, not 16–25).
H_MAX = (keys["year"] - keys["origin"]).groupby(keys["era"]).max().astype(int).to_dict()
if H_MAX["held"] != int(years[-1]) - min(D.held_out):
    raise ValueError("the held-out block's longest scored horizon is not the last data year minus its first origin")


def shown(era, b):
    """Band ``b``'s label in ``era``: cut at the era's longest scored horizon."""
    lo, hi = D.bands[BANDS.index(b)]
    return f"{lo}–{H_MAX[era]}" if lo <= H_MAX[era] < hi else b

Forecasts from the early origins, 1900–1950, outside the regime of modern mortality decline, under-predict life expectancy most: the flow field’s mean error at 36–50 years ahead is −7.7 to −2.0 years. Among the late origins, those around 1970 are a turning point: from 1965, 1970 and 1975 the flow field’s mean error is −2.36, −4.27 and −3.01 years, while from 1955, 1960 and 1985 it is within a year of the outcome (0.13, −0.20 and 0.75). Among the late origins the comparators in the table also under-predict most from 1970; anchored MDMx’s persists after it (−3.77 at 1980, −3.07 at 1985). The methods that extrapolate recent rates of improvement under-predicted from 1965–1975, while the naive, a linear trend in e₀ over each population’s whole history, over-predicted from every late origin that reaches these horizons (by 3.3 to 5.4 years). In the literature’s account, the data of the origins 1965–1975 end in the stall of adult male mortality of the 1950s and 1960s, just before the sustained decline of old-age, mostly cardiovascular, mortality from about 1970.

15.4 Predictive intervals

Each entry is scored with its own predictive distribution (paper §10.4): MDMx’s delta-method intervals scaled by κ; the flow field’s empirical quantiles of its own errors; Lee–Carter’s k_t interval mapped through e₀(k); the functional models’ simulations; bayesLife’s MCMC; the naive’s normal random walk; and the ensemble’s average of its members’ quantiles. MDMx’s κ and the flow field’s error quantiles are calibrated within era, leaving out the origin being calibrated; the held-out origins are calibrated on the late development origins only. Leave-one-origin-out calibration uses the errors of other origins, later ones included. The flow field’s quantiles, by horizon and sex, are then near nominal on the development origins by construction; MDMx’s κ, one factor pooled over horizons 1–50 and centred, is not, so its coverage by horizon is a finding. The held-out block tests both on outcomes mostly outside the calibration.

The flow field’s intervals, calibrated by horizon within the era, cover close to their nominal level there by construction; anchored MDMx’s, scaled by one factor pooled over every horizon, do so as a finding. Anchored MDMx’s 80 % intervals cover 81 % of the late-era outcomes and the flow field’s 78 %. Lee–Carter’s intervals, from its own k_t model, come close too (82 % with the last 50 years). The functional models’ simulated intervals are far too narrow (Hyndman–Ullah 46 %, the coherent model 50 %), and bayesLife’s, fitted to every year, too wide (97 %). The held-out block, below, tests the calibrated intervals on outcomes mostly outside their calibration: of the late-era points whose errors calibrate them, 16 % have outcome years that the block also scores.

15.5 The overall comparison

The overall comparison (the article’s §10.5–10.6; the detail is in this chapter only) ranks the entries on five families of measures, each counting a quantity once:

  • level: the MAE of female e₀ and of male e₀ (each sex once);
  • gap: the MAE of the female − male gap;
  • age-specific sex differences: the RMSE of the male − female difference in logit q_x, each age weighted by the observed deaths d_x;
  • age pattern: the RMSE of logit q_x weighted by the observed deaths, and the MAE of life expectancy at 65 for each sex;
  • intervals: the weighted interval score of female and of male e₀, every entry’s intervals made by one rule: the empirical quantiles of its own errors at the other origins of its era, later ones included (the held-out origins: the late era’s). The median of such an interval is the forecast shifted by the median error of those origins, so this family scores the calibrated dispersion of a bias-adjusted forecast, not the entry’s own statement of its uncertainty; that is tested by the coverage of each entry’s own intervals (above) and, on outcomes mostly outside the calibration, in the held-out block.

Each measure is divided by the naive’s value of the same measure, so 1 is the naive’s level, and a family’s loss is the mean of its measures. The entries are ranked over draws of family weights (Dirichlet(1, …, 1)), each draw with a bootstrap of population families: stochastic multicriteria acceptability analysis (SMAA). The full-output composite uses all five families; the e₀-only composite the level, the gap and the intervals. The families are not independent: across the entries the interval losses follow the level losses closely (the correlations below). Bias is not a measure: MAE contains it, and a bias term beside MAE rewards errors that offset (bias is reported by era, band and origin above). bayesLife enters the schedule families through its MortCast schedules.

Deviation 2. This is not the overall comparison of the frozen design. Two independent reviews of that design, made after the held-out block had been scored, found that the level of e₀ was counted in three overlapping families (about 60 % of the expected weight), that its bias terms rewarded offsetting errors, that its survivor-weighted age measures were dominated by noise at young ages, and that the methods’ own intervals were calibrated in different ways or not at all. The revision was made for these reasons; its effects on the ranking follow the headline below. The frozen comparison is reported beside this one as the record of the path.

The views: the primary view (late era, 1–15 years) decides the headline; the secondary view (early era, 1–15 years) is the out-of-regime check; the eras pooled; a sensitivity at 16–25 years in the late era; and, scored once, the held-out block.

COMPOSITES = {"full": "Full output", "e0": "e₀ only"}
VIEW_ORIGINS = {"late": ["late"], "early": ["early"], "development": list(D.eras), "held": ["held"]}
MAIN = {"families": EO["families"], "full": EO["composite_full"], "e0": EO["composite_e0"]}
FROZEN = {"families": OV["families"], "full": OV["composite_full"], "e0": OV["composite_e0"]}


def view_values(vals, view=None, spec=None):
    """The points of a view: by name (``[evaluation.views]``) or by its spec (origins, horizons)."""
    spec = spec or E["views"][view]
    lo, hi = spec["horizons"]
    return vals[vals["era"].isin(VIEW_ORIGINS[spec["origins"]]) & vals["h"].between(lo, hi)]


def rank(vals, comp, design=MAIN, methods=ENTRIES, bootstrap=True):
    return cp.overall(vals, design["families"], design[comp], methods=methods, naive=ev.NAIVE,
                      draws=int(OV["draws"]), seed=int(OV["seed"]), bootstrap=bootstrap)


def report_overall(overall, prefix, what):
    for (view, comp), r in overall.items():
        word = "".join(w.capitalize() for w in view.split("_")) + ("Full" if comp == "full" else "Ezero")
        pos = ev.rank_positions(r["mean_rank"])
        for label in ENTRIES:
            latex.report(f"evFirst{prefix}{word}{TAG[label]}", 100 * r["first"][label], digits=0,
                         desc=f"{label}: share (%) of SMAA draws ranked first, {COMPOSITES[comp]}, view {view}{what}")
            latex.report(f"evRank{prefix}{word}{TAG[label]}", r["mean_rank"][label], digits=2,
                         desc=f"{label}: mean SMAA rank, {COMPOSITES[comp]}, view {view}{what}")
            latex.report(f"evPlace{prefix}{word}{TAG[label]}", int(pos[label]),
                         desc=f"{label}: position by mean SMAA rank, {COMPOSITES[comp]}, view {view}{what}")


VIEWS = [v for v in E["views"] if v != "held_out" or HELD]
OVERALL = {(view, comp): rank(view_values(VALS, view), comp) for view in VIEWS for comp in COMPOSITES}
OVERALL_FROZEN = {(view, comp): rank(view_values(VALS_OWN, view), comp, FROZEN) for view in VIEWS for comp in COMPOSITES}
report_overall(OVERALL, "", "")
report_overall(OVERALL_FROZEN, "Frozen", " (the frozen design)")
latex.report("evDraws", int(OV["draws"]), desc="SMAA draws (weights and bootstrap)")

def view_name(view):

def overall_table(overall):
    """One row group per view; each composite's share of first places and mean rank under a spanner."""

                             for comp in COMPOSITES for k in ("1st (\\%)", "mean rank")}}
                         for view in VIEWS for label in ENTRIES])

Two of the flaws the reviews found, measured in the primary view: the losses of the frozen design’s three families that score the level of e₀ (e₀, the sexes and the intervals) correlate 0.91 to 0.93 across the entries, and its survivor-weighted age measures put 88 % of their squared error on ages 1–49, where deaths are few.

On forecasts from origins 1955–2000 at horizons of 1–15 years, the flow field ranks first in the overall comparison of age-specific and summary forecasts (86% of the draws), ahead of anchored MDMx, which ranks 3rd when fitted to all years and 4th when fitted to the last 50. In the early era (origins 1900–1950), the flow field ranks first (55%); anchored MDMx ranks 4th when fitted to all years and 2nd when fitted to the last 50. Under the frozen design: on forecasts from origins 1955–2000 at horizons of 1–15 years, the flow field ranks first in the overall comparison of age-specific and summary forecasts (100% of the draws), ahead of anchored MDMx, which ranks 3rd when fitted to all years and 4th when fitted to the last 50.

By mean rank the runner-up in the primary view is bayesLife fitted to the last 50 years. In the early era the flow field is first both in the most draws and by mean rank (1.98). The share of first places counts draws of family weights and of population families; it does not cover the uncertainty from the few late origins, whose outcome years overlap (a bootstrap of origins and leaving one origin out, in the robustness checks below).

The revision changed the flow field’s share of first places: in the primary view it is 86 % against 100 % under the frozen design, and on the held-out block 94 % against 97 %.

On e₀ alone the flow field ranks first in 49 % of the draws. Anchored MDMx’s mean rank on the full output is 3.66 with every year and 3.69 with the last 50 years; the ensemble’s 3.88.

The SMAA’s details for the primary view: each entry’s family losses on the whole sample (1 is the naive’s level), the share of draws in which its composite loss is below the naive’s, and, for the entries that ever rank first, the mean family weights of the draws in which they do (central weights). Then every measure on its own, so that a family average cannot hide a measure on which an entry is worse than the naive, and the probability that each entry’s composite loss is below each other’s.

Its male e₀ error is 1.11 times the naive’s, and it beats the naive on male e₀ in 28 % of the populations (AvgRelMAE 1.23). 15.5.1 Robustness of the ranking

The same comparison in other cuts (paper §10.7), to show what decides it: each horizon band of the primary view on its own (the per-band comparison specified in advance), the late era at 26–50 years (descriptive: no forecast there was ever tested out of sample), a bootstrap of origins instead of population families (the late origins share period shocks), every population weighted equally, and the three total series whose parts are also scored left out.

15.5.2 Sensitivities

Each sensitivity (paper §10.7) changes one thing and ranks the entries again in the primary and secondary views. None is used for the headline.

  • The frozen design (as pre-registered; the table above).
  • Each method’s own intervals instead of the one rule.
  • Survivor weights for the age measures (as in the frozen design), and the age family without the old-age measure.
  • Bias added back, without cancellation: the level and gap families also get the mean over origin × horizon-band cells of the absolute mean error.
  • Without the interval family, which partly re-scores the level of the errors (the correlations above).
  • The ensemble with the naive as a fourth member.
  • α_k = 1 for the forecasts that start beyond the frontier point: these jobs keep their deviations from the shape law unrelaxed.
  • MDMx with the decaying anchor (half-life 2 years), and unanchored, in place of anchored MDMx fitted to all years.
  • The comparators averaged across windows: each comparator’s forecast is the mean over the windows 25, 50, 75, 100 years and all years (development origins only).
  • The comparators’ actual jump-off: Lee–Carter and Hyndman–Ullah started from the observed rates of the jump-off year (jumpchoice = "actual"; the coherent model has no such option), as MDMx and the flow field start from their observed jump-off.
  • The ages from 100 as one open interval: the comparators forecast one rate for the open interval and their schedules repeat it at every older age, so the age measures, summed over single ages, count that one forecast once per age. Here the schedule and sex-difference measures fold those ages into one cell, the logit of the probability of dying between that age and the last age of the table, for every entry, the naive and the truth alike; e₆₅ is unchanged.
  • Intervals from past errors only: every entry’s intervals from its errors at the earlier origins whose outcome had been observed by the origin (described with the interval checks below), in place of the within-era rule, on the points where every entry has one.
  • Leave one origin out: the range of each entry’s share of first places when each origin of the view is left out in turn.
The sensitivities: rank again with one thing changed 
z_obs_keys = np.moveaxis(M[:, :, keys["pop"].map({p: i for i, p in enumerate(pops)}).to_numpy(),
                           (keys["year"] - years[0]).to_numpy()], -1, 0)


def scored(z, at=None):
    """The schedule measures of schedules ``z`` aligned to ``at`` (default: the common points)."""
    at = keys if at is None else at
    zo = z_obs_keys if at is keys else np.moveaxis(
        M[:, :, at["pop"].map({p: i for i, p in enumerate(pops)}).to_numpy(), (at["year"] - years[0]).to_numpy()],
        -1, 0)
    return at.assign(**ev.schedule_measures(z, zo, GROUPS, OLD_AGE))


def replaced(changes):
    """The primary and secondary views ranked again with some entries' points and schedule measures replaced;
    their intervals by the one rule, from their new errors."""
    pts, q, sc_ = ev.with_changes(points, Q_RULE, sched, {lab: (p, None, s) for lab, (p, s) in changes.items()})
    new = [lab for lab, (p, _) in changes.items() if p is not None]
    if new:
        qn, _ = ev.empirical_quantiles(pts, truth, keys, new, calibration=CAL, pi_levels=F["pi_levels"],
                                       min_points=MIN_PTS)
        q.update(qn)
    vals, _ = ev.complete(ev.point_values(pts, truth, keys, q, sc_, LEVELS, FAMILY, D))
    return {(view, comp): rank(view_values(vals, view), comp) for view in ("primary", "secondary")
            for comp in COMPOSITES}


def with_families(families, vals=VALS, drop=()):
    """The primary and secondary views with other families of measures, or without the families ``drop``."""
    design = {**MAIN, "families": families, **{c: [f for f in MAIN[c] if f not in drop] for c in COMPOSITES}}
    return {(view, comp): rank(view_values(vals, view), comp, design) for view in ("primary", "secondary")
            for comp in COMPOSITES}

                        for o, r in runs["comparators"]["full"].items()},
                str(D.window): {o: fc.comparator_points(r, code, A, ctx["cmp"]["mx_to_qx_ax"])

                            for o, r in curve[w]["comparators"].items()} for w in curve}}
    dev = sorted(set.intersection(*(set(v) for v in variants.values())))
    avg_pts = ev.ensemble_points({w: ev.long_points({"x": {o: v[o] for o in dev}}).drop(columns="entry")
                                  for w, v in variants.items()})
    # A window can fail where another does not (Lee–Carter on Iceland's last 25 years at 1925 and
    # 1930): the average exists only where every window has a schedule.
    dev_keys = keys[keys["origin"].isin(dev)]
    for v in variants.values():
        dev_keys = dev_keys.merge(pd.concat([r["schedule_index"][["pop", "year"]].assign(origin=int(o))
                                             for o, r in v.items() if o in dev]), on=["pop", "origin", "year"])
    dev_keys = dev_keys.reset_index(drop=True)
    print(f"{name} averaged across windows: {int(keys['origin'].isin(dev).sum()) - len(dev_keys)} development "
          "points without a schedule in some window")
    avg_z = sum(cp.aligned_schedules({o: v[o] for o in dev}, dev_keys) for v in variants.values()) / len(variants)
    avg_changes[f"{name}, all years"] = (avg_pts.assign(h=avg_pts["year"] - avg_pts["origin"]), scored(avg_z, dev_keys))
SENS["comparators averaged across windows"] = replaced(avg_changes)

    return "; ".join(f"{ev.entry_phrase(lead)} ranks first in {WHERE[view]} with "

                     for lead, g in ch.groupby(f"{view}: first", sort=False))

15.5.3 Bias with and without cancellation

Bias is not a measure of the comparison, but how much a pooled bias hides matters for reading it: biases of opposite sign at different origins or horizons cancel in a mean over a whole view. The table sets the absolute mean error over a view beside the mean, over the cells of origin and horizon band, of the absolute mean error in each.

Code

for view in ("primary", "secondary"):

                     view)
    for label in ENTRIES + [ev.NAIVE]:
        e_ = v_[v_["method"] == label]

15.5.4 The anchor’s residual and the sex differences by age

Both anchored forecasters carry the jump-off residual, the part of the jump-off year’s observed schedule that the scores do not represent, smoothed over age (Section 14.2.5). Unsmoothed, the residual would hold the noise of that one year’s single-age rates as well as the population’s own detail, and the forecasts would carry it at every horizon. Which measures such noise reaches depends on how they weigh the errors over age. The measure of the sex differences by age squares the error at each age and so charges single-age noise in full; the gap in e₀ sums the errors over the ages, so noise of opposite signs at neighbouring ages cancels and what remains is the systematic part. To show what the smoothing does, the anchored forecasts are scored again on the primary view’s points with the residual as observed, the forecast change of the scores left as it is. This is a sensitivity, not an entry of the comparison.

The anchored forecasters with the jump-off residual as observed, beside the entries and bayesLife (each measure divided by the naive’s)

With the residual as observed, the flow field would score 0.95 of the naive’s error on the sex differences by age and anchored MDMx 0.93 (all years), close to the observed jump-off schedule held fixed, 0.93: unsmoothed, the jump-off year’s noise would dominate the measure. With the residual smoothed they score 0.80 and 0.78, against bayesLife’s 0.88 (last 50 years) and 0.87 (all years), and the age pattern improves with them (the flow field 0.82 against 0.89), while the flow field’s female and male e₀ hardly move (0.64 and 0.77 against 0.64 and 0.78). Much of what is left is noise of the outcome year: the observed schedules themselves, smoothed over 7 ages, score 0.48. bayesLife’s schedules come from MortCast fitted to smoothed rates, so their sex difference is smooth across ages, but their systematic error is larger: the mean error of the difference at ages 0–39 is 0.14 in logit(q_x) for bayesLife fitted to the last 50 years and 0.02 for the flow field, and 59 % of bayesLife’s squared error lies at ages 90 and over, where its schedules repeat the rate of the open age group.

15.6 Variants and benchmarks beside the comparison

The comparison ranks the twelve entries fixed in the frozen design. Beside it, never ranked and reported in full only in the companion, are the forms and benchmarks the independent reviews asked for. Each is computed and scored at the development origins only (1900–2000, both eras), on the comparison’s own points, so that the held-out block stays reserved for the ranked entries:

  • the flow field’s other forms: FR0-all, whose speed beyond the frontier point stays at its value there, and FR2-all, the form the frontier rule as written chose (Deviation 1), both with every part estimated on every year;
  • a drop-one-component ablation of FR1-50, whose plan was committed before its results;
  • Li–Lee’s coherent model in two forms: the group form, in which the origin’s populations share a common factor for each sex, and the sex-coherent form, in which the two sexes of a population share one;
  • anchored MDMx fitted to every year with other drift weights and numbers of components.

No choice of form or design depends on these results.

The unranked variants at the development origins (cached per origin; computed ahead by tools/warm_variants.py)

            "deaths_common": "the common factor's index is refitted to the group's deaths",

                "deaths_common": "the common factor refitted to deaths", "none": "no index refitted"}[LL["refit"]]
VRES = va.variant_results(VRUNS, n_ages=A, ax=ctx["cmp"]["mx_to_qx_ax"],
                          lilee_codes={"group": LL["method_group"], "sex": LL["method_sex"]})
KEYS_DEV = va.development_keys(keys, D)
# The variants' FR1-50 is the ranked entry, to the last digit.
_ref = ev.long_points({"x": VRES[va.FLOW_REFERENCE]})
_ent = ev.long_points({"x": results["Flow field"]})
_ref = _ref.merge(_ent, on=["pop", "sex", "origin", "year"], suffixes=("", "_entry"), validate="one_to_one")
if len(_ref) != len(ev.long_points({"x": VRES[va.FLOW_REFERENCE]})) or (_ref["e0_fc"] != _ref["e0_fc_entry"]).any():
    raise ValueError("the variants' FR1-50 is not the ranked flow field")
VTAG = {"FR1-50": "FrOneFifty", "FR0-all": "FrZeroAll", "FR2-all": "FrTwoAll", "no frontier rule": "NoFrontier",
        "no shape law": "NoShape", "deviations persist": "Persist", "deviations vanish": "Vanish",
        "no anchor": "NoAnchor", va.LILEE_LABELS["group"]: "LlGroup", va.LILEE_LABELS["sex"]: "LlSex",
        "MDMx, drift weights 1/0": "MdmxHmdHundred", "MDMx, drift weights 0.5/0.5": "MdmxHmdFifty",
        "MDMx, drift weights 0.2/0.8": "MdmxHmdTwenty", "MDMx, 3 components": "MdmxPcThree",
        "MDMx, 7 components": "MdmxPcSeven"}
missing_tag = sorted(set(VRES) - set(VTAG))
if missing_tag:
    raise ValueError(f"no macro tag for the variants {missing_tag}")
ll_fail = {code: pd.concat([r["failures"] for r in by_o.values()], ignore_index=True)
           for code, by_o in VRUNS["lilee"].items()}
for code, fails in ll_fail.items():
    latex.report(f"evLilee{'Group' if code == LL['method_group'] else 'Sex'}Failures", len(fails),
                 desc=f"Li-Lee ({code}): populations not forecast at a development origin")
fr2_flow = pd.DataFrame({o: r["runs"]["FR2-all"]["flow"] for o, r in VRUNS["flow"].items()}).T
latex.report("evFrTwoFallbacks", int(fr2_flow["fallback"].astype(bool).sum()),
             desc="FR2-all: development origins at which its rule fell back to FR0")
print(f"Variants: {len(VRES)}; Li-Lee failures {[len(f) for f in ll_fail.values()]}; "
      f"development points {len(KEYS_DEV):,}")


def variant_bands(entries, common=True):
    """Band errors of the named variants and entries on the comparison's development points."""
    pick = {lab: (VRES[lab] if lab in VRES else results[lab]) for lab in entries}
    return va.band_errors(pick, truth, KEYS_DEV, D, M, pops, years, GROUPS, old_age=OLD_AGE, common=common)


def report_bands(tab, labels, prefix, what, stats=(("mae", "Mae"), ("me", "Bias")), measure="e0_both"):
    """Macros ev<prefix><Mae|Bias><tag><Era><Band> of one measure of a band table."""
    for stat, word in stats:
        wide = va.band_wide(tab, measure, stat, D, labels)
        for lab in labels:
            for era in D.eras:
                for b in BANDS:
                    v = wide.loc[lab, (era, b)]
                    if np.isfinite(v):
                        latex.report(f"ev{prefix}{word}{VTAG.get(lab, TAG.get(lab))}{ERA_TAG[era]}{BAND_TAG[b]}", v,
                                     digits=2, desc=f"{what}: {stat} of {measure}, {lab}, {era} era, horizons {b}")


def bands_out(tab, labels, measures=(("e0_both", "mae", "e0 MAE"), ("e0_both", "me", "e0 bias"))):
    """A band table for the paper in long form: (measure, era, entry) × horizon band."""
    rows = [va.band_wide(tab, measure, stat, D, labels).xs(era, axis=1, level=0)
            .assign(Measure=name, Era=era).rename_axis("Entry").reset_index()
            for measure, stat, name in measures for era in D.eras]
    return pd.concat(rows, ignore_index=True)[["Measure", "Era", "Entry", *BANDS]]


def below(w, a, others, era):
    """The bands of ``era`` in which row ``a`` of a band table (:func:`mdmx.variants.band_wide`) is below
    every row of ``others``."""
    others = [others] if isinstance(others, str) else list(others)
    return [b for b in BANDS if w.loc[a, (era, b)] < w.loc[others, (era, b)].min()]


def above(w, a, others, era):
    """The bands of ``era`` in which row ``a`` of a band table is above every row of ``others``."""
    others = [others] if isinstance(others, str) else list(others)
    return [b for b in BANDS if w.loc[a, (era, b)] > w.loc[others, (era, b)].max()]


def plain(label):
    """A measure's label without LaTeX, for the prose: "female $e_{65}$" → "female e₆₅"."""
    sub = str.maketrans("0123456789", "₀₁₂₃₄₅₆₇₈₉")
    return re.sub(r"\$e_\{?(\d+)\}?\$", lambda m: "e" + m.group(1).translate(sub), label)


def bands_text(bs):
    """Horizon bands as words."""
    if len(bs) == len(BANDS):
        return "at every horizon band"
    if not bs:
        return "at no horizon band"
    return "at " + (", ".join(bs[:-1]) + " and " if len(bs) > 1 else "") + bs[-1] + " years"

In the late era FR1-50’s MAE is below both other forms’ at every horizon band; in the early era it is above both at every horizon band. At 36–50 years in the late era FR2-all, the written rule’s choice, has a mean error of 3.10 years and FR0-all, whose speed beyond the frontier point stays at its value there, one of −3.36, against −1.83 for FR1-50.

What each part of FR1-50 contributes: the same forecaster with one part dropped at a time, every measure that its plan named. The plan fixed in advance that no change of form follows from the ablation.

Code 
ABL = [va.FLOW_REFERENCE, *va.ABLATION]
abl_tab, abl_used = variant_bands(ABL)
ABL_MEASURES = {("e0_both", "mae"): "MAE of $e_0$", ("e0_both", "me"): "Mean error of $e_0$",
                ("e0_female", "mae"): "MAE of female $e_0$", ("e0_female", "me"): "Mean error of female $e_0$",
                ("e0_male", "mae"): "MAE of male $e_0$", ("e0_male", "me"): "Mean error of male $e_0$",
                ("gap", "mae"): "MAE of the gap", ("schedule_dx", "mae"): "RMSE of the schedule (deaths)",
                (f"e{OLD_AGE}_female", "mae"): f"MAE of female $e_{{{OLD_AGE}}}$",
                (f"e{OLD_AGE}_male", "mae"): f"MAE of male $e_{{{OLD_AGE}}}$"}
rows_ = []
for (measure, stat), name in ABL_MEASURES.items():
    w = va.band_wide(abl_tab, measure, stat, D, ABL)
    for era in D.eras:
        rows_.append(w.xs(era, axis=1, level=0).assign(Era=era, Measure=name).reset_index())
ABL_OUT = pd.concat(rows_, ignore_index=True).rename(columns={"entry": "Variant", "index": "Variant"})
ABL_OUT = grouped_bands(ABL_OUT[["Measure", "Era", "Variant", *BANDS]], "Variant")
save_table(ABL_OUT, "tbl-ev-ablation",
           "What each part of the flow field contributes (the ablation): FR1-50 "
           "(the ranked entry) and the same with one part dropped: no frontier rule (the speed held at "
           "$g(s_1^*)$ beyond the frontier point), no shape law (the other scores held at their jump-off "
           "values), deviations persist ($\\alpha_k = 1$), deviations vanish ($\\alpha_k = 0$), no anchor (no "
           "jump-off residual).  MAE and mean error (years; the schedule RMSE in logit units, weighted by the "
           f"observed deaths) by era and horizon band, on the {latex.fmt_int(int(abl_used['scored'].min()))} "
           "common points at origins 1900--2000.",
           short_caption="The ablation of the flow field", formats=formats(ABL_OUT, 2), groups="Group",
           spanners=": ", rank=ranked_bands(ABL_OUT, stub="Variant"),
           rank_note=RANK_BANDS.replace("smallest MAE", "smallest MAE or RMSE"))
report_bands(abl_tab, va.ABLATION, "Abl", "Ablation")
report_bands(abl_tab, va.ABLATION, "Abl", "Ablation", stats=(("mae", "GapMae"),), measure="gap")
report_bands(abl_tab, va.ABLATION, "Abl", "Ablation", stats=(("mae", "SchedRmse"),), measure="schedule_dx")
AW = va.band_wide(abl_tab, "e0_both", "mae", D, ABL)
# Bands at which dropping the part raises the e0 MAE (FR1-50 below the variant).
ABL_HURTS = {era: {v: len(below(AW, va.FLOW_REFERENCE, v, era)) for v in va.ABLATION} for era in D.eras}
for era, by_v in ABL_HURTS.items():
    for v, n in by_v.items():
        latex.report(f"evAblHurts{VTAG[v]}{ERA_TAG[era]}", n,
                     desc=f"Ablation, {v}: horizon bands (of {len(BANDS)}) at which the e0 MAE rises, {era} era")
# Strictly below FR1-50 at every band (ties and missing bands do not count).
ABL_GAINS = {era: [v for v in va.ABLATION if len(below(AW, v, va.FLOW_REFERENCE, era)) == len(BANDS)]
             for era in D.eras}


def hurts_text(era):
    return "; ".join(f"{v}, {n}" for v, n in ABL_HURTS[era].items())


def gains_text():
    parts = [f"in the {era} era " + " and ".join(f'"{v}"' for v in vs) + " lowers the MAE at every band"
             for era, vs in ABL_GAINS.items() if vs]
    return ("Of the dropped parts, " + "; ".join(parts) + ".") if parts else ""

Dropping one part raises the e₀ MAE (average of the sexes) at this many of the 6 horizon bands. Late era: no frontier rule, 6; no shape law, 6; deviations persist, 0; deviations vanish, 6; no anchor, 3. Early era: no frontier rule, 0; no shape law, 5; deviations persist, 6; deviations vanish, 4; no anchor, 6. Of the dropped parts, in the early era “no frontier rule” lowers the MAE at every band; in the late era “deviations persist” lowers the MAE at every band. As the ablation’s plan fixed in advance, no change of form follows from these results.

Li–Lee’s two forms beside Lee–Carter, the same model without a common factor, and the coherent functional model, on the points every one of them forecasts. Li–Lee is fitted to the last 50 years, and the common factor’s index is refitted to the group’s life expectancy, as Li and Lee (2005) published it.

Code

           "of the gap (years), and the schedule RMSE (logit, deaths-weighted), by era and horizon band, on the "
           f"{latex.fmt_int(int(ll_used['scored'].min()))} points at origins 1900--2000 that every one of them "
           "forecasts.", short_caption="Li--Lee beside the comparators", formats=formats(LL_OUT, 2),

           rank_note="among the five methods in each column of each group, the best being the smallest MAE or RMSE")

report_bands(ll_tab, LL_SET[:2], "Var", "Li-Lee", stats=(("mae", "GapMae"),), measure="gap")

Every measure of the comparison for each variant, relative to the naive on the same points, in the primary and secondary views; population by population (AvgRelMAE of the mae: and rmse: measures) as macros.

Code 
VVALS = va.variant_values(VRES, truth, keys, D, M, pops, years, GROUPS, old_age=OLD_AGE, levels=LEVELS,
                          pi_levels=F["pi_levels"], calibration=CAL, min_points=MIN_PTS, families=FAMILY)
CODES = [c for f in MAIN["full"] for c in MAIN["families"][f]]
vm_rows, rel_rows = [], []
for view in ("primary", "secondary"):
    base_v, var_v = view_values(VALS, view), view_values(VVALS, view)
    r_ = va.ratios_to_naive(base_v, var_v, families=MAIN["families"], composite=MAIN["full"], naive=ev.NAIVE)
    vm_rows.append(r_.assign(view=view, worse=(r_[CODES] > 1).sum(axis=1)))
    for lab in var_v["method"].unique():
        v_ = var_v[var_v["method"] == lab]
        both_, _ = ev.complete(pd.concat([v_, base_v[(base_v["method"] == ev.NAIVE) & base_v["point"].isin(v_["point"])]],
                                         ignore_index=True))
        rel_rows.append(ev.relative_errors(both_, [lab], ev.NAIVE, [c for c in CODES if c.split(":")[0] in ("mae", "rmse")])
                        .assign(view=view))
VM = pd.concat(vm_rows, ignore_index=True)
VREL = pd.concat(rel_rows, ignore_index=True)
VM_OUT = VM[["view", "method", "points", *CODES, "worse"]].rename(

The comparison’s intervals are calibrated on the other origins of the era, later ones included, so they use errors that had not been observed by the origin. Intervals from past errors only use, at origin o and horizon h, only the errors at earlier origins o′ whose outcome had been observed by the origin (o′ + h ≤ o), where at least 20 such errors exist. The two rules are compared on the points where both give an interval; the early era has few, because its first origins have no earlier errors.

Code 
PAST = "past errors"    # the rule's label in the table and the macros' descriptions (RT_Q: the sensitivities)
IC = va.interval_comparison({"within era": Q_RULE, PAST: RT_Q}, keys, truth, D, F["pi_levels"],
                            {"1–15": (1, 15)})
ic = IC[(IC["sex"] == "both") & (IC["span"] == "1–15")]

IC_OUT = IC_OUT.reindex(index=ENTRIES + [ev.NAIVE])
IC_OUT = IC_OUT[[(st, e, r) for e in D.eras for r in ("within era", PAST) for st in ("in80", "in95", "wis")]
                + [("n", e, PAST) for e in D.eras]]
for st in ("in80", "in95"):
    IC_OUT[[c for c in IC_OUT.columns if c[0] == st]] *= 100
RULE_HEAD = {"within era": "Within the era", PAST: "Past errors only"}
STAT_HEAD = {"in80": "80 %", "in95": "95 %", "wis": "WIS", "n": "Points"}

    [pd.DataFrame({f"{RULE_HEAD[r]}: {STAT_HEAD[st]}": IC_OUT[(st, e, r)] for (st, e_, r) in IC_OUT.columns

     for e in D.eras], ignore_index=True)
IC_OUT = IC_OUT[["Era", *[c for c in IC_OUT.columns if c != "Era"]]]
save_table(IC_OUT, "tbl-ev-past-intervals",
           "Intervals from past errors only: each entry's empirical quantiles from its errors at the earlier origins whose "
           "outcome had been observed by the origin ($o' + h \\le o$), at least "
           f"{MIN_PTS} errors per cell, against the comparison's within-era rule (the other origins of the era, "

           "interval score (years) of $e_0$, the average of the sexes, horizons 1--15, on the points where both "

                                                                                 if c.endswith("Points")])
           | {c: "{:.0f}" for c in IC_OUT.columns if c.endswith("%")}, groups="Era", spanners=": ",
           rank=[ranked(IC_OUT, {c: (int(c[-4:-2]) if c.endswith(" %") else "min") for c in IC_OUT.columns
                                 if c.endswith((" %", "WIS"))})],

                     "the nominal level and the smallest score (the naive is not ranked)")
for r_ in ic.itertuples():
    rule = "Past" if r_.rule == PAST else "We"
    for lev in F["pi_levels"]:
        latex.report(f"ev{rule}Cov{TAG[r_.entry]}{ERA_TAG[r_.era]}{LEVEL_TAG[lev]}", 100 * getattr(r_, f"in{lev}"),
                     digits=0, desc=f"Coverage (%) of the {lev} % interval, {r_.rule} rule, {r_.entry}, {r_.era} era, "

    latex.report(f"evPastPoints{ERA_TAG[era]}", n_rt,

RT = ic.pivot_table(index="entry", columns=["era", "rule"], values=["in80", "wis"], sort=False)
for era in D.eras:

        latex.report(f"ev{tag}CovEightyMin{ERA_TAG[era]}", c80.min(), digits=0,

             else f"for {RT_WIDER['late']} of the {len(RT)} forecasters, the naive included")

Intervals from past errors only draw on every earlier origin, early-era ones included, so in the late era they cover more: their 80 % intervals cover 80–91 % of the outcomes, against 77–79 % within era, and their interval score is higher for every one of the 13 forecasters, the naive included. The lowest interval score belongs, in the late era, to the flow field from past errors only and bayesLife fitted to the last 50 years within era; in the early era, to the flow field, under both rules.

At the ages where small populations record zero deaths, chapter d5 pools deaths and exposures over blocks of adjacent years formed on the whole series. A block can therefore span a forecast origin, and a job’s jump-off year can then share data with years after the origin (disclosed, not changed). The counts, and the primary view’s comparison again without the populations whose jump-off year is pooled with later years at a late-era origin (descriptive).

Without the 9 populations (788 points of the primary view), the flow field ranks first in 65 % of the draws and bayesLife fitted to the last 50 years in 16 %. Without only their 23 late-era jobs whose jump-off year is pooled with later years (328 points), the flow field ranks first in 72 %. On the held-out view, without the 20 populations with a pooled jump-off at a held-out origin (528 points), the flow field ranks first in 89 % of the draws; without only their 37 jobs (324 points), the flow field in 93 %. These checks remove data along with the leak, so they show how far the comparison rests on these populations and jobs. Two more measure it. The first scores every entry, as forecast, against the HMD’s published tables (the curated tables without pooling) instead of the comparison’s truth: it shows how much the pooled truth itself changes the scores.

Code 
DP = P.section("data")
LT_CUR = artifacts.load("lt_curated")["lt"]
LT_POOL = artifacts.load("lt_pooled")
LABELS_EV = artifacts.load("event_labels")
TRUTH_UN = va.unpooled_truth(LT_CUR, LABELS_EV, artifacts.load("populations"), artifacts.load("tensor"),
                             q_min=float(DP["q_min"]), min_observed_years=int(DP["min_observed_years"]))
POOLED_JOBS = POOL["jobs"][["pop", "origin"]].drop_duplicates().assign(pooled=True)


def e0_both_errors(pts, tr):
    e_ = ev.errors(pts, tr, keys)
    e_ = e_[(e_["measure"] == "e0_both") & e_["h"].between(1, 15)].assign(era=lambda d: d["origin"].map(ERA_OF))
    return e_.merge(POOLED_JOBS, on=["pop", "origin"], how="left").assign(pooled=lambda d: d["pooled"].fillna(False))


ERR_PO, ERR_UN = e0_both_errors(points, truth), e0_both_errors(points, TRUTH_UN)
TRUTH_DIFF = ERR_PO.merge(ERR_UN, on=["entry", "pop", "origin", "year", "h", "measure", "era", "pooled"],
                          suffixes=("_po", "_un"), validate="one_to_one")
TRUTH_DIFF["d_truth"] = TRUTH_DIFF["error_un"] - TRUTH_DIFF["error_po"]      # pooled truth − published truth
PT_ERAS = ["late", "held"] if HELD else ["late"]
pt_rows = []
for label in ENTRIES + [ev.NAIVE]:
    row = {"Entry": label}
    for era in PT_ERAS:
        for sub, mask in (("pooled jump-off", True), ("every point", None)):
            if era == "held" and sub == "every point":
                continue
            d_ = TRUTH_DIFF[(TRUTH_DIFF["entry"] == label) & (TRUTH_DIFF["era"] == era)]
            if mask:
                d_ = d_[d_["pooled"]]
            row[f"{ERA_HEAD[era]}, {sub}: Truth"] = d_["error_po"].abs().mean()
            row[f"{ERA_HEAD[era]}, {sub}: Published"] = d_["error_un"].abs().mean()
    pt_rows.append(row)
PT_OUT = pd.DataFrame(pt_rows)
# Short group heads for the page (a long head widens its two narrow columns past the text width).
PT_TEX = PT_OUT.rename(columns=lambda c: c if c == "Entry" else
                       c.replace(", pooled jump-off:", ", pooled:").replace(", every point:", ", all points:"))
save_table(PT_TEX, "tbl-ev-pool-truth",
           "The pooled truth: each entry's MAE of $e_0$ (the average of the sexes, horizons 1--15) against the "
           "comparison's truth (the pooled tables; Truth) and against the HMD's published tables after the "
           "curation (Published): in the late era on the jobs whose jump-off year is pooled with years after "
           "the origin (pooled) and on every point (all points), and at the recent origins on the jobs with a "
           "pooled jump-off.  The forecasts are those of the comparison.",
           short_caption="The pooled truth", spanners=": ", formats=formats(PT_TEX, 2), colsep=4)
for era in PT_ERAS:
    tag = ERA_TAG[era]
    pj = TRUTH_DIFF[(TRUTH_DIFF["era"] == era) & TRUTH_DIFF["pooled"] & (TRUTH_DIFF["entry"] == ev.NAIVE)]
    latex.report(f"evPoolTruthDiff{tag}", float(pj["d_truth"].abs().mean()), digits=2,
                 desc=f"Mean |e₀ of the pooled truth − e₀ of the published table| (years), {era}, the points of the "
                      "jobs whose jump-off is pooled with later years, horizons 1–15")
    lower = [lab for lab in ENTRIES
             if PT_OUT.set_index("Entry").loc[lab, f"{ERA_HEAD[era]}, pooled jump-off: Truth"]
             < PT_OUT.set_index("Entry").loc[lab, f"{ERA_HEAD[era]}, pooled jump-off: Published"]]
    latex.report(f"evPoolTruthLower{tag}", len(lower),
                 desc=f"Entries (of 12) whose e₀ MAE on the pooled jobs ({era}) is lower against the pooled truth")
    chg = (PT_OUT.set_index("Entry").loc[ENTRIES, f"{ERA_HEAD[era]}, pooled jump-off: Published"]
           - PT_OUT.set_index("Entry").loc[ENTRIES, f"{ERA_HEAD[era]}, pooled jump-off: Truth"])
    latex.report(f"evPoolTruthChangeMin{tag}", float(chg.min()), digits=2,

    latex.report(f"evPoolTruthChangeMax{tag}", float(chg.max()), digits=2,

ALL_CHG = (PT_OUT.set_index("Entry").loc[ENTRIES, f"{ERA_HEAD['late']}, every point: Published"]
           - PT_OUT.set_index("Entry").loc[ENTRIES, f"{ERA_HEAD['late']}, every point: Truth"])
latex.report("evPoolTruthChangeAllLate", float(ALL_CHG.abs().max()), digits=3,
             desc="Largest |change| of an entry's e₀ MAE over every late-era point (1–15), published minus pooled truth")

Against the published tables the entries’ MAE on these jobs changes by 0.01 to 0.04 years (12 of the 12 entries do better against the pooled truth), and over every late-era point by at most 0.004.

The second removes the leak. At every origin the pooling of chapter d5 is planned again on the years up to the origin alone (the same valley ages and settings), and every entry whose inputs are pooled is forecast again from the result: the flow field and anchored MDMx from the tensor, Hyndman–Ullah and the coherent model from the rates smoothed after the same pooling, for the populations whose cells change. Lee–Carter and bayesLife’s e₀ read the unpooled rates and keep their forecasts; the ensemble is rebuilt from its members, and the naive is fitted to the published series. Every entry is then scored against the published tables, on e₀ and the point forecasts alone: the MAE by horizon band and the comparison on e₀ only, with the intervals of the comparison’s one rule from these errors.

15.6.1 Paired differences of the error

The SMAA ranks the entries over many measures at once. Beside it, one measure between two forecasters at a time: the MAE of e₀ (the average of the sexes) of the flow field minus that of another forecaster, on the late-era points where both are scored, in the first horizon bands. The late era’s origins share their periods, so the interval resamples whole origins (a block bootstrap); the share of draws below zero describes the resampling and is not a p-value. The other forecasters: the ensemble, bayesLife and anchored MDMx (ranked entries), Lee–Carter from the observed rates of the jump-off year (a sensitivity above) and FR2-all (a variant).

    return "; ".join(f"{ev.entry_phrase(b).replace(', actual jump-off', ' from the observed jump-off')} at "
                     f"{', '.join(g['band'])} years" for b, g in rows.groupby("b", sort=False)) or "no forecaster"

The bootstrap interval lies below zero (the flow field more accurate) against bayesLife fitted to the last 50 years at 6–10, 11–15 years; anchored MDMx fitted to all years at 1–5, 6–10, 11–15 years; FR2-all at 1–5, 6–10 years, and above zero against no forecaster. In the other cells it includes zero: with 10 origins resampled, those differences are not distinguished from the variation between periods.

15.7 Generality

Three properties of a general forecaster, in the companion only, for every entry but bayesLife and the ensemble:

  1. More history must not hurt: the MAE with every year minus the MAE with the last 50 years, at horizons up to 15, in each era, must not exceed the margin: twice the typical standard error of a regret between forecasters in that era and band (the median, over the other entries, of the standard error of the difference of MAE between the flow field and that entry, over a bootstrap of population families). For the flow field the comparison is with its windowed variant. The entry already estimates its shape law and its pace beyond the frontier point on the last 50 years, so this test varies the window of its remaining speed only; the window curve below varies every component.
  2. Stable structure across origins: the flow field’s frontier point, its speed there, its pace beyond, the shrinkage weight and the relaxation rates by origin (chapter 11, Table 14.1); MDMx’s damping ρ by origin (Table 15.31, after the generality table).
  3. Bounded regret out of era: each entry’s early-era MAE minus the best entry’s, by band.
Code

                               WM["bands"], multiplier=float(WM["multiplier"]), draws=int(WM["draws"]),
                               seed=int(WM["seed"]))

                 desc=f"Margin of the test that more history must not hurt (years), {r_['era']} era, horizons "

             "Lee–Carter": ("Lee–Carter, all years", "Lee–Carter, last 50 years"),

    e_all = dev_both[dev_both["entry"] == all_]
    e_win = ffw_err if win_ == "Flow field, windowed" else dev_both[dev_both["entry"] == win_]
    rob = ev.window_robustness(ev.band_table(e_all.assign(entry=name), D, ["entry", "era"]),
                               ev.band_table(e_win.assign(entry=name), D, ["entry", "era"]), MARGINS, ["entry"])
    row = {"Entry": name}
    for era in D.eras:
        r_ = rob[rob["era"] == era]
        row[f"{era}: largest excess"] = float((r_["diff"] - r_["margin"]).max())
        row[f"{era}: hurts"] = "yes" if bool(r_["hurts"].any()) else "no"
    grows.append(row)
early_bands = ev.regret(bands[(bands["era"] == "early") & bands["band"].isin(BANDS[:3])
                              & bands["entry"].isin(ENTRIES)])
reg = early_bands.pivot_table(index="entry", columns="band", values="regret", observed=True)
gen_tab = pd.DataFrame(grows)
for name, (all_, _) in [*gen_pairs.items(), ("Flow field", ("Flow field", None))]:
    for b in BANDS[:3]:
        gen_tab.loc[gen_tab["Entry"] == name, f"early regret {b}"] = reg.loc[all_, b]
GEN_OUT = gen_tab.rename(columns={
    **{f"{era}: largest excess": f"{ERA_HEAD[era]}: Largest\nexcess" for era in D.eras},
    **{f"{era}: hurts": f"{ERA_HEAD[era]}: Hurts" for era in D.eras},
    **{f"early regret {b}": f"Early-era regret: {b}" for b in BANDS[:3]}})

def hurt_text(era):
    """The comparators that more history hurts in ``era``, each with its largest excess over the margin."""
    names = {"Lee–Carter": "Lee–Carter", "Hyndman–Ullah": "Hyndman–Ullah", "Coherent FDM": "the coherent model"}
    parts = []
    for e, name in names.items():
        if era in HURTS[e]:
            key = f"evHistoryExcess{GEN_TAG[e]}{ERA_TAG[era]}"
            # An excess that prints as 0.00 is still above the margin: say so rather than print zero.
            by = "less than 0.01 years" if round(val(key), 2) == 0 else f"{num(key)} years"
            parts.append(f"{name} (by {by})")
    if not parts:
        return "none of the comparators"
    return parts[0] if len(parts) == 1 else ", ".join(parts[:-1]) + " and " + parts[-1]

More history does not hurt the flow field (largest excess of its error with every year over the margins −0.12 years in the early era and −0.06 in the late era; negative is inside) and does not hurt anchored MDMx (−0.10 and −0.05). Beyond the margin, more history hurts in the early era Lee–Carter (by 0.31 years), Hyndman–Ullah (by 0.43 years) and the coherent model (by 0.38 years), and in the late era Lee–Carter (by 0.01 years) and Hyndman–Ullah (by 0.02 years). Out of era, anchored MDMx fitted to the last 50 years and the flow field have the smallest early-era error in the bands up to 15 years; anchored MDMx’s regret is at most 0.40 years. MDMx’s damping factor is stable across origins (median 0.96 with every year and 0.88 with the last 50 years in the late era, 0.97 and 0.92 in the early era). With the last 50 years, the lower quartile sits at the bound of 0.80 at 5 of the 10 late origins (1955, 1960, 1965, 1970, 1975).

15.7.1 The window curve

Each entry (but bayesLife and the ensemble) fitted to its last 25, 50, 75 and 100 years and to every year (development origins). The flow field is windowed by component: its speed only, its shape law only, both, and both with the space estimated on the window too.

Anchored MDMx barely depends on its window: its late-era error at 1–15 years ranges from 0.90 to 0.92 years across the windows. In the late era Lee–Carter is best with 50 years (0.85, against 0.94 with every year and 1.05 with 25); in the early era all three comparators are best with the shortest window (Lee–Carter 1.99 with 25 years against 2.70 with every year). The flow field’s long-horizon error depends on the window of its shape law, in opposite directions in the two eras: at 16–50 years a shape law on the last 25 years gives 1.44 in the late era against 2.09 on every year, but 3.97 in the early era against 3.21. The entry’s form (the shape law on the last 50 years) gives 1.57 and 3.41.

What this says about the guiding principle of the forecasters, one general model that uses all the data (in the companion only). Its strong form, that a general model should not need to discard history, does not hold for the flow field: two of its three components, the shape law and the pace beyond the frontier point, use only the last 50 years, a window chosen on the late origins (Deviation 1), and the shape law’s window moves the error in opposite directions in the two eras. The narrowed form, pre-registered as the fallback, is that the weight of each datum reflects its relevance and may approach zero. The flow field meets it only coarsely: its window gives the older years a weight of zero, set by a choice rather than estimated in the model. Its remaining component, the speed, uses every year, and there more history does not hurt (the generality table).

15.8 Where the errors come from

The leaders’ e₀ pace over the 50 years before the origin was highest at 1960 (0.34 years of e₀ per year) and 0.17 at the last development origin. The flow field uses the same leaders’ pace in s₁, not in e₀; what it implies in e₀ is its gain 2–5 years ahead for the forecasts that start beyond the frontier point. That gain differed from the frontier’s realised pace over the next 25 years in both directions: it was below it at 15 of the 21 development origins, by up to 0.13 years per year (at 1930), and above it at the others, by up to 0.10 (at 1955); at the development origins from 1980 the two differ by at most 0.04.

def _space_seconds():
    """Seconds to estimate, at each origin, the space the two forecasters share (the flow field's runs above
    start from it; anchored MDMx's time includes it)."""
    import time
    ms_, rows_ = ctx["mdmx"], []
    for o in sorted(int(x) for x in runs["flowfield"]):
        w0, c0 = time.perf_counter(), time.process_time()
        fc.origin_space(M, observed, years, o, tau=ms_.tau, age_rank=ms_.age_rank, smooth=ms_.smooth, n_pc=ms_.n_pc)
        rows_.append({"origin": o, "seconds": time.perf_counter() - w0, "cpu_seconds": time.process_time() - c0})
    return pd.DataFrame(rows_)

The flow field takes 0.05 seconds per origin (all its populations, forecasts and schedules), and 0.09 with the space it shares with anchored MDMx (0.04 s). That is about 110 times faster than anchored MDMx, 210 times faster than the three R comparators together and 32,000 times faster than bayesLife, which takes 0.8 hours per run (median; the longest 1.9; 42.0 run-hours for its 48 runs).

The other methods’ times are those of the render that computed them, on this book’s machine (Apple M1 Max, 10 cores, macOS 27.2.1). bayesLife’s 48 runs were made by the off-site batch on two machines: 3 on Apple M1 Max, 10 cores, 3 at a time (this book’s reference machine); 45 on Apple M4 Max, 16 cores, 5 at a time. Each bayesLife run’s three chains run in parallel; MDMx’s fits run in parallel worker processes; the R comparators run as one R session per origin for all three methods. Runs shared cores, so the times are indicative; the differences between the methods are of orders of magnitude.

15.10 The held-out block

The origins 2005–2015 (paper §10.1 and §10.6) were held out from every formal choice of form and design (what had been seen there is listed with the design above). They were scored once, under the frozen design, by the run that set score_held_out = true and changed nothing else, as the design required. The overall comparison was revised afterwards (Deviation 2) and corrected (Deviation 3), so the revised comparison’s held-out view, reported first below, is not a blind test of the revised design; the frozen design’s view is reported beside it. The block reaches at most 20 years ahead, so this section reports the primary view’s comparison and the bands up to that horizon.

The held-out block: scored only when score_held_out is true
